summary: At just 2.6 square miles, East Palo Alto is smaller than many regional parks yet packs nearly 30,000 residents at a density north of 11,000 per square mile — placing it among the most tightly knit patches of the San Francisco Peninsula, wedged between the Baylands salt marshes to the east and the conspicuous wealth of Palo Alto and Menlo Park to the south and west. The terrain is dead flat, barely above sea level, and the western edge sits close enough to Meta's sprawling headquarters campus in Menlo Park that some commutes are bikeable, while Stanford, the VA hospital system, and a constellation of tech employers are all within a short drive — yet a home-price-to-income ratio above 10:1 means that even at the local median household income of roughly $105,000, purchasing a median-priced home ($1.124 million) requires substantial outside capital or dual high-earning households. Renters face $2,209 monthly at the median, consuming about 25 percent of that same household income — tight but technically within conventional affordability thresholds. The climate is classically mild Bay Area: average highs around 69°F year-round with over nine hours of daily sunshine, rarely requiring heating or cooling. The Ravenswood Open Space Preserve and Bay Trail segments offer flat, wind-swept walks along the shoreline with wide views across the South Bay, though the city's interior grid is more utilitarian than scenic, bisected by University Avenue's commercial corridor. East Palo Alto sits at a striking geographic seam — surrounded by some of the most expensive zip codes on Earth, sharing their climate and proximity to major employers, yet carrying a median home value roughly half that of its immediate neighbors, a gap that defines almost every conversation about the city's future.
